470.title: Dattatreya's last teacher: the wasp
470.hook: a wandering sage's last teacher is a wasp, and under Patanjali's strangest powers runs the same rule: you become what you dwell on
470.carry: you become what you dwell on
470.tomorrow: Dhruva, the boy who became the pole star
470.howItsDone: Hindus practice japa, repeating a name of God, and keep a chosen form of God before the eyes in puja, trusting the old teaching that the mind takes the form of what it dwells on; in the Yoga tradition, the classical commentators treat the siddhis as real attainments, while some modern teachers read them symbolically.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Krishna and his poor friend's handful of rice. A mood can be known; its reason is theirs.
screen: `THE HANDFUL OF RICE — A MOOD, NOT ITS REASON.`

segments.voice: On day four hundred thirty-nine you met Dattatreya, the wandering sage who named twenty-four teachers, among them an arrow-maker who never looked up. The last teacher on his list is the strangest. A wasp, the Bhagavata says, carries a small grub into its mud nest and shuts it in. The grub, trapped, thinks of nothing but the wasp, out of sheer fear. And in the old telling, it thinks so hard that it becomes a wasp itself. Old India believed that about the potter wasp. The lesson was never really about bugs.
screen: `A SAGE WITH TWENTY-FOUR TEACHERS.` → `THE LAST ONE: A WASP.` → `THE GRUB BECOMES WHAT IT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Here's what Dattatreya learns. Whatever a person fixes the whole mind on, out of love, hatred or fear, that person comes to take its form. It's one of Hinduism's big ideas: you become what you dwell on. You've met it before. On day one eighty-seven, King Bharata's last thought was a deer. On day four forty-two, Narada said even Kamsa reached Krishna, by fear. Now Patanjali builds powers on the same rule. Sutra 3.21: by samyama on the body's form, the yogi can't be seen. Antardhana, disappearing. Sutra 3.23: by samyama on friendliness and the others, their strengths. Those are the four attitudes from book one: friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity. Sutra 3.24: by samyama on strengths, the strength of an elephant. The classical commentators take these as real powers, and some in the tradition still do. Some modern teachers read them as pictures of the wasp's rule: hold friendliness completely, and you grow friendly; hold strength, and you grow strong. And invisibility? One reading: the ego that no longer needs to be noticed. This is why Hindus keep a name of God going under the breath, japa, and set a form of God before the eyes in puja. Not to impress anyone. To grow like what they love. So it's worth asking, honestly, what you dwell on most. The feed you scroll last thing at night is a kind of wasp too.
screen: `THE WASP AND THE GRUB.` · `LOVE, HATRED, FEAR: THE MIND TAKES ITS FORM.` · `3.23: FRIENDLINESS, ITS STRENGTH.` · `3.24: THE ELEPHANT'S STRENGTH.` · `JAPA: THE RULE, USED ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `YOU BECOME WHAT YOU DWELL ON.`

segments.voice: Choose one name to dwell on: Ram, Krishna, Om namah Shivaya, whatever your family says. Repeat it softly or silently with the breath. If you don't pray, rest on friendliness instead, the warmth you'd feel greeting an old friend at the door. When the mind wanders, come back to the name, or the warmth. You're becoming what you hold.
Invisibility. Antardhana in Sanskrit, the first power in today's sutras. One reading: what disappears is the need to be seen.

471.title: Dhruva, the boy who became the pole star
471.hook: a five-year-old's prayer holds so steady that Vishnu sets him in the sky, and it's why a Hindu couple is shown the pole star
471.howItsDone: Dhruva's story is commonly told to Hindu children, Narada's twelve-syllable mantra to Vishnu is widely chanted, and in many Hindu weddings the couple is shown the pole star as a sign of a steady marriage; teachers of the Yoga Sutras read 3.26–3.29 as samyama moving from the sky to the body's center.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dattatreya's wasp, and the rule under the powers. You become what you dwell on.
screen: `THE WASP — YOU BECOME WHAT YOU DWELL ON.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata tells of a boy named Dhruva. He's five. He climbs onto his father the king's lap, and his stepmother pulls him off: if you wanted that lap, she says, you should have been born to me. He runs to his mother, crying. She doesn't fight back. She tells him only the Lord can give him a place no one can take. So the five-year-old walks into the forest to find the Lord.
screen: `A BOY PULLED OFF A LAP.` → `INTO THE FOREST.` → `TO FIND THE LORD.`

segments.voice: On the way, the sage Narada tests him: you're a child, go home. Dhruva won't. So Narada gives him a mantra, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, and a way to sit. Dhruva prays by the Yamuna for months, eating less and less, until he stands on one foot, and the story says the whole world feels his weight. Vishnu comes. And here's the turn: Dhruva finds he no longer wants what he came for. He went looking for a lap and found the Lord. Vishnu gives him a place anyway, the star that never moves, the one point the whole night sky turns around. Dhruva means fixed, steady. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, steadiness is itself devotion, and God answers a prayer that doesn't move, even a child's. You can see it at a Hindu wedding. In many weddings, the priest shows the couple the pole star, Dhruva, as a picture of a marriage that holds. Now Patanjali points samyama at the sky. Sutra 3.26, on the sun: knowledge of the worlds. 3.27, on the moon: how the stars are arranged. 3.28, on the pole star: how they move. Fix on the one point that doesn't move, and you can read the motion of everything else. Then 3.29 comes down to the body's own center, the navel. It's why so many Hindus keep one prayer every single day, the way Dhruva kept his mantra. When a week won't stop moving, that prayer is the point that doesn't.
screen: `NARADA'S MANTRA.` · `A PRAYER THAT DOESN'T MOVE.` · `VISHNU: THE FIXED STAR.` · `THE WEDDING: SHOWN THE POLE STAR.` · `3.28: REST ON WHAT'S STILL.` · then, large: `DEVOTION THAT DOESN'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: Let your attention rest on one point. If you pray, make it the name Narada gave Dhruva, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, said slowly. If you don't, make it the navel, rising and falling with the breath. Thoughts will move around it like the night sky turning. You don't have to stop them. Stay with the one point, and watch the rest move.
Dhruva: fixed, steady. The pole star, and the boy who became it, with a prayer that didn't move.

472.title: Hanuman's heart
472.hook: Hanuman opens his chest to show who lives there, and Patanjali sends you to the heart to know your own mind
472.tomorrow: Fourteen years to walk on water
472.howItsDone: Many Hindus meditate on their chosen form of God seated in the heart, and pictures of Hanuman opening his chest to show Rama and Sita hang in homes and temples; teachers of the Yoga Sutras read 3.34 alongside the Upanishads' lotus of the heart.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dhruva, devotion that doesn't move, set in the sky as the pole star.
screen: `DHRUVA — DEVOTION THAT DOESN'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: The war is over. Rama is crowned in Ayodhya, and Sita gives Hanuman a gift, a necklace of pearls. Hanuman takes it, and in front of the whole court, starts biting the pearls open, one by one, peering inside each. People laugh. Someone asks what on earth he's doing. Looking for Rama, he says. Anything without Rama in it is worth nothing to me. So, they ask, is Rama in you? Hanuman tears open his chest. And there, in his heart, sit Rama and Sita.
screen: `A NECKLACE OF PEARLS.` → `BITTEN OPEN, ONE BY ONE.` → `RAMA AND SITA, IN HIS HEART.`

segments.voice: That scene isn't in Valmiki's Ramayana. It comes from later, much-loved tellings, and it's painted on calendars and temple walls wherever Hanuman is loved. It pictures one of Hinduism's deepest teachings: God lives in the heart. In the Gita, Krishna says the Lord dwells in the heart of every being. On day three fifty-six you met the Upanishad's picture: the body as the city of Brahman, and in it a small lotus-house, the heart, with a space inside as wide as the sky. Now Patanjali. After the sky and the navel, samyama climbs: 3.30, on the hollow of the throat, hunger and thirst cease; 3.32, on the light in the crown, the vision of the perfected ones. Then 3.34: hridaye chitta-samvit. In the heart, knowledge of the mind. Chitta is the whole field of thinking and feeling. Rest attention in the heart, and you come to know it. The classical commentary reads the sutra through that same lotus-house in the city of Brahman. So to know your own mind, the tradition doesn't send you to think harder. It sends you to the heart, where, many Hindus say, God is already sitting. Hanuman didn't have to argue for his love. He only had to show what lived there. And today, when you're trying to work out what you really want, ask what lives in your heart. That's what's running the mind.

segments.voice: Put a hand on the center of your chest and feel it rise and fall. Let your attention settle there, not in the head. If you pray, picture the form of God you love seated there, the way Hanuman held Rama and Sita. If you don't, picture a small lotus with a quiet space inside. When thoughts come, watch them from the chest.
The heart. Hridaya: where samyama gives knowledge of the mind, and where Hanuman kept Rama and Sita.

473.title: Fourteen years to walk on water
473.hook: a man spends fourteen years learning to walk on water, and Hindu teachers say even real powers stand in the way
473.carry: the powers are obstacles, not the goal
473.howItsDone: Teachers in Hindu yoga and devotional lineages quote sutra 3.37, and Krishna's words to Uddhava in the Bhagavata, to warn students against chasing powers; the aim is moksha, or God, not the abilities that may come along the way.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's heart. God lives in the heart, and resting there, you come to know the mind.
screen: `HANUMAN'S HEART — GOD LIVES THERE.`

segments.voice: Ramakrishna, the nineteenth-century saint of Bengal, liked to tell a story. A man goes off alone to the forest and practices hard for fourteen years. At last he can walk on water. Overjoyed, he hurries to his teacher to show him. And the teacher says, gently: my poor child. What took you fourteen years, ordinary people do for a penny. They pay the boatman. Ramakrishna's point wasn't that the power was fake. It was that it was beside the point.
screen: `FOURTEEN YEARS IN THE FOREST.` → `HE WALKS ON WATER.` → `THE BOATMAN CHARGES A PENNY.`

segments.voice: Patanjali says the same thing, right in the middle of his list of powers. Sutra 3.37: te samadhav upasarga vyutthane siddhayah. These are obstacles in samadhi; to the outward-turned mind, they're powers. Siddhi means an accomplishment. Upasarga means an obstacle, a trouble that comes at you. Patanjali uses both words for the very same things. The difference is where you stand. Facing the world, hearing what no one else can hear looks like a prize. In samadhi, it's one more thing to look at, when the whole point was to rest as the seer. And it isn't only Patanjali. In the Bhagavata, in his last long talk with his friend Uddhava, Krishna lists eighteen powers a yogi can gain, and then says it outright: for one who is seeking me, these are obstacles, and a waste of time. That's the teaching, in the yoga schools and the devotional ones alike. The goal is moksha, freedom, or God himself. Not powers. Notice Patanjali doesn't call them fake. He keeps listing them for the rest of book three. He just tells you plainly what they cost if you chase them. Today the powers look smaller: followers, being impressive, the clever answer. Ramakrishna would ask the same question about those. Did it take you fourteen years to cross a river you could have crossed for a penny?
screen: `UPASARGA: AN OBSTACLE.` · `SIDDHI: AN ACCOMPLISHMENT.` · `SAME THINGS, TWO NAMES.` · `KRISHNA TO UDDHAVA: A WASTE OF TIME.` · then, large: `THE POWERS ARE OBSTACLES, NOT THE GOAL.`

segments.voice: Rest on the breath, or on a name of God if you pray. Sooner or later a pleasing thought arrives: something you did well, a compliment, a clever idea. Notice how it tugs, wanting to be looked at. Don't push it away. Nod to it, like the boatman's penny, and come back to the breath, or the name.
Upasarga, an obstacle, a trouble that comes at you. In the outward mind the powers are accomplishments; in absorption, they're in the way.
screen: `UPASARGA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the powers are obstacles, not the goal. Freedom is the goal. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 473 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SHANKARA IN THE KING'S BODY.`

474.title: Shankara in the king's body
474.hook: Shankara leaves his body in a cave and lives as a king, and behind the story sits an old teaching: you are not your body, or even your mind
474.carry: you wear the body; you are the seer
474.howItsDone: Hindus widely teach that the self (atman) is not the body, a teaching voiced in the Bhagavad Gita and behind belief in rebirth; the classical commentaries on the Yoga Sutras treat these powers as real within the Samkhya-Yoga view, and the traditional life of Shankara tells of one used briefly and set aside.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: fourteen years to walk on water. The powers are obstacles, not the goal.
screen: `THE BOATMAN'S PENNY — POWERS AREN'T THE GOAL.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells a story about the great teacher Shankara. He has just won a famous debate against the scholar Mandana Mishra, and Mandana's wife, the brilliant Ubhaya Bharati, takes up the challenge herself. She asks him about love between husband and wife. Shankara, a lifelong monk, has no answer. So he asks for time. He leaves his own body in a cave, guarded by his students, and enters the body of a king who has just died. He lives as that king for a while, learns what he needs, and comes back. Today's sutras name that very power, and others just as startling.
screen: `A DEBATE ABOUT LOVE.` → `A MONK WITH NO ANSWER.` → `HE ENTERS A KING'S BODY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.38: by loosening what binds the mind to one body, and knowing the mind's pathways, the mind can enter another body. Para-sharira-avesha. More follow. 3.39: master udana, the upward breath, and the body rises. 3.40: master samana, the breath at the center, and a radiance. The classical commentators read these as real. They can, because of what Hindu thought says a person is. In the Samkhya-Yoga picture, the body is made of nature, prakriti. So is the mind, just far subtler. That's how a mind might move from one body to another, the way Shankara did. But neither one is you. You are the seer, purusha, the one who watches body and mind. The Upanishads call it atman, the self. And the Gita gives the picture every Hindu child hears: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new. That's what Hindus mean by rebirth. It's also why, at a Hindu funeral, many families say the one who wore the body has gone on. Shankara, in the story, didn't stay a king. He learned what he came for, and went back to his own body and his work. Today that's worth remembering on the days the body feels like everything: a mirror, an illness, an age. You wear it, and it matters. It isn't the whole of you.

475.title: Hanuman's eight powers
475.hook: Hanuman holds all eight powers and still calls himself Rama's servant; the master, the commentary says, leaves the world's order alone
475.carry: hanuman's way: power in God's service
475.howItsDone: Many Hindus sing the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, honoring Hanuman as the giver of the eight siddhis and the model of devoted service (dasya bhakti); in the Yoga tradition, the eight powers of 3.45 are understood as fruits of mastery that a practitioner is warned not to pursue for their own sake.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shankara in the king's body. You wear the body; you are the seer.
screen: `SHANKARA — YOU ARE THE SEER.`

segments.voice: In the Ramayana, Hanuman has to cross the ocean to find Sita. He grows enormous, a mountain of a monkey, and leaps. When he reaches Lanka, he needs the opposite, so he shrinks, small enough to slip past the guards at nightfall. Vast when the task is vast. Tiny when the task is tiny. And when the demons finally spot him, he doesn't boast about any of it. He roars his name for them: I am the servant of Rama.
screen: `HANUMAN GROWS VAST.` → `THEN SMALL ENOUGH TO SLIP IN.` → `I AM RAMA'S SERVANT.`

segments.voice: That's the teaching under every Hanuman shrine: the mightiest one in the story calls himself a servant. Hindus call it dasya bhakti, loving God the way a devoted servant loves the one he serves, and Hanuman is its great model. His power is never for himself. Now Patanjali names powers like Hanuman's. Sutra 3.44: by samyama on the five elements, earth, water, fire, air and space, mastery of the elements. Bhuta-jaya. Sutra 3.45: from that mastery comes minuteness and the rest. The commentary lists eight: becoming tiny, becoming light, becoming vast, reaching anything, getting what one wills, control, lordship, and fulfilling one's resolve. The Hanuman Chalisa, sung in homes and temples, calls Hanuman the giver of those eight powers. Sutra 3.46 adds the body's perfection: beauty, grace, strength, and a hardness like diamond. Then the commentary says something worth keeping. Such a yogi could overturn the order of things, and doesn't, because that order was set by the will of one perfected long before. Later commentators name that one Ishvara, the Lord. Total mastery, and the master serves an order bigger than himself. That's Hanuman. And remember 3.37: chased for themselves, even these are obstacles. Hanuman never chased his. So whatever strength you've got, a talent, a voice, arms that can carry things, Hanuman's question is simple: whose service is it in?
screen: `DASYA BHAKTI: THE SERVANT'S LOVE.` · `BHUTA-JAYA: MASTERY OF ELEMENTS.` · `TINY, LIGHT, VAST: THE EIGHT.` · `THE MASTER LEAVES THE ORDER ALONE.` · then, large: `POWER IN GOD'S SERVICE.`

segments.voice: If you pray to Hanuman, say his name slowly, or a line of the Chalisa you know. If you don't, feel the five elements in your body: earth in your weight on the seat, water in your mouth, fire in your warm hands, air in the breath, space in the chest. Then, in your mind, offer that strength to something bigger than you.
Bhuta-jaya, mastery of the elements. It brings the eight powers and the body's perfection: beauty, grace, strength and diamond hardness.
screen: `BHUTA-JAYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Hanuman's way, power in God's service. All eight powers, and he called himself a servant. Until tomorrow.

476.title: King Ambarisha's senses
476.hook: a king who could have any pleasure gives each of his senses to God, and it's why a puja has a lamp, a bell, incense, flowers and food
476.carry: master the senses by offering them
476.howItsDone: A Hindu puja engages every sense, with lamp, bell, incense, flowers, sandal paste and food offered and received back as prasad; devotional teachers point to King Ambarisha as the model of senses turned toward God, and yoga teachers present 3.47 as samyama on perception itself.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhuta-jaya, and Hanuman's way: power in God's service. All eight powers, and he called himself a servant.
screen: `HANUMAN — POWER IN GOD'S SERVICE.`

segments.voice: You met King Ambarisha on day one thirty, keeping his Ekadashi fast while an angry sage raged. The Bhagavata says he ruled the whole earth. Any pleasure a king could want was his for the asking. Here's what he did with his senses. His eyes he gave to seeing Vishnu's images. His ears, to hearing Vishnu's stories. His hands, to cleaning Vishnu's temple. His nose, to the scent of tulsi from Vishnu's feet. And his tongue, to tasting food first offered to God.
screen: `A KING WITH EVERY PLEASURE.` → `EYES, EARS, HANDS.` → `EVERY SENSE GIVEN TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Ambarisha didn't shut his senses down. He turned them. That's the Hindu teaching about the senses. The Katha Upanishad calls them horses: strong, and the work is to steer them, not to kill them. Patanjali calls it indriya-jaya, mastery of the senses. Sutra 3.47: by samyama on the senses in five aspects, mastery. Not just what you see, but the seeing itself; the sense of me that says I see; and what the senses are for. Sutra 3.48: from that comes a swiftness like the mind, and mastery over nature itself. One way to read book three: it walks from the outside in. yesterday the elements, what's known; today the senses, the knowing; tomorrow, the one who knows. The devotional path does it Ambarisha's way. Look at a Hindu puja: a lamp for the eyes, a bell for the ears, incense and flowers for the nose, food offered and shared back as prasad for the tongue, sandal paste and flowers, offered by hand, for touch. Many teachers read it as every sense brought to God at once. Now the week. Dattatreya's wasp. Dhruva's steady star. Hanuman's heart. The walker on water. Shankara in a king's body. Hanuman's service. And Ambarisha. A week of powers, and every story points past them. Today your senses get pulled all day, by screens built to catch them. Ambarisha's answer isn't to close your eyes. It's to give them something worth seeing.
screen: `AMBARISHA: SENSES TURNED, NOT SHUT.` · `THE KATHA: SENSES AS HORSES.` · `INDRIYA-JAYA: MASTERY OF SENSES.` · `LAMP, BELL, INCENSE, PRASAD.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `MASTER THE SENSES BY OFFERING THEM.`

segments.voice: If you have a lamp or a candle, light it; if not, picture one. Give it your eyes for a moment. Then your ears: one sound around you. Then smell, taste and touch: the air, your own mouth, your hands resting. If you pray, offer each sense to God as you go, the way Ambarisha did. If you don't, simply give each one your full attention.
Indriya-jaya, mastery of the senses. By samyama on the senses in five aspects, it brings a swiftness like the mind's own.
screen: `INDRIYA-JAYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: master the senses by offering them. Ambarisha turned every one toward God. A week of the powers, done.
